samples.summary: SSRF guard only inspects IP literals, so a public DNS name that resolves to the metadata endpoint (e.g. `169.254.169.254.nip.io`) is fetched — defeating the protection the README/design doc advertise
samples.evidence:
`assertFetchableImageUrl` ends with `if (isPrivateHost(url.hostname)) throw` (image-fetcher.ts:186). `isPrivateHost` only matches loopback *names* (`localhost`, `*.localhost`) and IP *literals* (image-fetcher.ts:74-102); any other hostname falls through and is fetched.

Attack chain, fully traced: (1) an attacker who can write document content — another workspace member, a shared doc, or an agent generating content — sets an image inline `src` to `http://169.254.169.254.nip.io/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role>` (nip.io/sslip.io are public wildcard DNS that resolve the embedded literal; `metadata.google.internal` and bare single-label intranet names work the same way). (2) The victim runs `wafflebase docs export <id> out.docx` (packages/cli/src/commands/docs.ts:261) or `slides export` (commands/slides.ts:209), which builds the fetcher and passes it into `DocxExporter.export` / `PdfExporter.export`. (3) `resolveImageUrl` passes the absolute URL through unchanged; `assertFetchableImageUrl` sees hostname `169.254.169.254.nip.io`, which is not in `LOOPBACK_HOSTS`, does not end in `.localhost`, and does not match the IPv4 or IPv6 literal regexes — so no throw. (4) `fetchImpl(current, {redirect:'manual'})` (image-fetcher.ts:221) issues the GET from the operator's machine, and `res.blob()` (line 232) hands the response body to the exporter, which streams it verbatim into the DOCX zip / PDF image stream. The credentials therefore land in the exported file the attacker can later request.

The code comment at image-fetcher.ts:160-162 acknowledges this as a limitation, but README.md and docs/design/cli.md §10 both present the guard as the thing that stops an image `src` aiming an export at `169.254.169.254`, and the refusal message even names the escape hatch — so operators will read this as covered. A guard that reads as covering the named attack while a one-token DNS trick walks around it is worse than none. Closing it needs DNS resolution plus connect-time address pinning (e.g. a custom undici dispatcher/`lookup` that re-checks the resolved address), not a hostname string test.

samples.summary: `isPrivateHost` omits several non-public IPv4 ranges and the IPv4-compatible IPv6 spelling
samples.evidence: The IPv4 branch (image-fetcher.ts:88-96) covers 0/8, 10/8, 127/8, 169.254/16, 172.16-31, 192.168/16 and 100.64-127, but not 192.0.0.0/24 (IETF protocol assignments), 198.18.0.0/15 (benchmarking), 192.0.2.0/24 / 198.51.100.0/24 / 203.0.113.0/24 (TEST-NET), 224.0.0.0/4 (multicast) or 240.0.0.0/4 (reserved). Separately, `unwrapIpv4Mapped` (line 110) only folds the `::ffff:` mapped form; the deprecated IPv4-*compatible* spelling `http://[::a9fe:a9fe]/` (i.e. `::169.254.169.254`) reaches `isPrivateHost` as `::a9fe:a9fe`, matches none of the IPv6 tests at lines 98-100, and is allowed. Exploitability of the IPv4-compatible form is low (most stacks will not route it to the v4 address), which is why I rate this minor rather than folding it into the DNS finding, but the ranges above are reachable on real internal networks.

samples.summary: `printDryRun`'s dot-segment backstop misses percent-encoded dot segments, so a caller that forgets `seg()` can still get a walked-out URL printed as "the request that would be sent"
samples.evidence: `assertNoDotSegments` (dry-run.ts:44-52) compares each `/`-split part against the literal strings `'.'` and `'..'`. Per the WHATWG URL spec a double-dot path segment is `..`, `.%2e`, `%2e.` or `%2e%2e` (ASCII case-insensitive), and a single-dot segment is `.` or `%2e` — `new URL('https://h/a/%2e%2e/b').pathname` is `/b`. The check is documented (dry-run.ts:15-18) as the backstop for a *future* call site that forgets `seg()`; that is exactly the caller most likely to hand the printer an already-percent-encoded id read from a file or an agent payload. Such a path passes the backstop and `printDryRun` prints a URL that normalizes to an endpoint outside `/api/v1/workspaces/<ws>` — the one output an agent is most likely to copy and run. The real request path is unaffected because `seg()` escapes `%` (`seg('%2e%2e')` → `%252e%252e`); only the backstop is weak. Fix: decode/normalize each segment, or compare against `/^(\.|%2e){1,2}$/i`.

samples.summary: `safeEnvelope` sanitizes only `code` and `message`; arbitrary upstream sibling fields such as `error.command` are forwarded to agent stderr unbounded and unfiltered
samples.evidence: `safeEnvelope` builds `const error = { ...body.error, code }` (formatter.ts:163) and then clamps only `message` (line 164-166). Every other key the upstream put inside `error` is forwarded verbatim, subject only to the 4 KB whole-body cap at line 168. `ApiError` declares `command?: string` (packages/cli/src/client/http-client.ts:31) and README.md/docs/design/cli.md describe `command` as a hint worth keeping — i.e. a field an agent reading the envelope is invited to act on. An upstream that is not fully trusted (a MITM on a plain-`http` `--server`, a self-hosted or misconfigured backend, or a `--server` pointed at an attacker) can therefore place attacker-chosen text into a field an agent may treat as a suggested next command, while the HTML-rejection and 500-char clamp that protect `message` do not apply. Consider clamping every string value in the spread, or whitelisting `{code, message, command}` with `clampUpstreamText` applied to each.

samples.summary: The browser export image fetcher issues credentialed GETs to any document-controlled `src`, and the change's "same rule applies to the frontend" pass did not touch it
samples.evidence: `docsImageFetcher` does `fetch(resolveImageUrl(url), { credentials: 'include' })` (export-utils.ts:49-51) on an image `src` that is document content — the same untrusted input the CLI guard was added for. There is no scheme or address check: `resolveImageUrl` passes any absolute URL through (line 15), so a doc-supplied `src` of `http://127.0.0.1:9200/...` or `http://intranet-admin/...` produces a credentialed GET from the victim's browser when they export. Cross-origin CORS stops the *response* from being read, so this is request-side-effect only (a GET-triggered action on an intranet host), which is why I rate it minor with low confidence. I flag it because the design doc explicitly generalizes the CLI's hardening to the browser client ("The rule is not CLI-only") and applies `seg()` to every frontend API module, while leaving the analogous document-controlled fetch unguarded — a reader of the doc will believe the browser side is covered. Searched: grepped `fetch(` and `VITE_BACKEND_API_URL`/`BACKEND_BASE` across packages/frontend/src, read export-utils.ts and app/spreadsheet/image-upload.ts; found no equivalent of `assertFetchableImageUrl` anywhere in packages/frontend.

verdict.reason: Verified in the repository. `isPrivateHost` (image-fetcher.ts:74-102) only tests hostname strings: exact loopback names (LOOPBACK_HOSTS, line 67), a `.localhost` suffix (line 83), an IPv4 dotted-quad regex (line 85), and IPv6 literal patterns (lines 98-100). A public DNS name that resolves to a private address (e.g. `169.254.169.254.nip.io`, `metadata.google.internal`) matches none and returns false. `assertFetchableImageUrl` ends with `if (isPrivateHost(url.hostname)) throw` (line 186) and has no deny-by-default, so the URL is accepted and fetched at line 221 with the body returned to the exporter at line 232 — landing metadata-endpoint responses inside the exported DOCX/PDF. Reachable from `docs export` (commands/docs.ts:261, used at 279/289/294/305) and `slides export` (commands/slides.ts:209-210), both on untrusted document content per the module's own comment (lines 142-146). No mitigating guard exists elsewhere: `sameOriginAsServer` (184) and `isAllowedHost` (138) are allow short-circuits, not extra denials, and no DNS/connect-time pinning exists. Refutation grounds do not apply: the code is present as described (not `not-present`), nothing guards it upstream (not `already-guarded`), and SSRF is explicitly named in this lens's lane (not `out-of-scope`). I discounted one overstated part of the reviewer's rationale — docs/design/cli.md:1143-1145 does explicitly caveat that this is "not a full SSRF defense"; only packages/cli/README.md:35-38 omits it — but a documented limitation does not refute the vulnerability, and the code comment at lines 160-162 is an acknowledgement rather than a mitigation.

finding.summary: New SSRF guard is bypassable by an HTTP redirect — `fetch` follows redirects by default and the allow-list is only checked on the initial URL
finding.evidence: `assertFetchableImageUrl(resolved, opts.serverBase)` runs once, before `await fetchImpl(resolved)` (image-fetcher.ts:151-152). Node/undici `fetch` defaults to `redirect: 'follow'` and does not re-invoke any caller-side check on the redirect target. Attack: a workspace member (or an agent-generated doc) sets an image inline `src` to `https://attacker.example/x.png`; the guard sees a public https host and allows it; the attacker's server answers `302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`. `wafflebase docs export` / `slides export` running on an operator's cloud instance then GETs the metadata endpoint and embeds the response bytes into the exported PDF/DOCX/PPTX. The doc comment enumerates the residual gap as only "a public hostname that resolves to a private address" (line 107-109) — redirects are not mentioned and not handled, so the guard reads as covering a case it does not. Fix would be `redirect: 'manual'` plus re-running `assertFetchableImageUrl` on each `Location`.

verdict.reason: The claimed code does not exist. `createImageFetcher` does not call `fetchImpl(resolved)` with default redirect following: line 221 passes `{ redirect: 'manual' }`, lines 222-224 detect 301/302/303/307/308 via REDIRECT_STATUSES (line 46), line 240 resolves the Location against the current URL, and line 241 re-runs `assertFetchableImageUrl(next, opts.serverBase, allowedHosts)` on every hop, with a 5-hop cap at lines 235-239. The doc comment also explicitly covers redirects at lines 156-158 ("re-runs this on every redirect target, because `fetch` follows redirects itself and would otherwise let a public host hand the export a `Location:` pointing at the metadata endpoint"); the residual-gap paragraph at 160-162 correctly limits itself to DNS-resolution rebinding. The exact 302-to-169.254.169.254 attack is refused at line 241 via isPrivateHost (line 91), and a regression test exists at packages/cli/test/image-fetcher.test.ts:257. Both production entry points (packages/cli/src/commands/docs.ts:261 and packages/cli/src/commands/slides.ts:209) construct the fetcher through createImageFetcher, so no unguarded path exists. The reviewer's suggested fix is exactly what the code already implements.

finding.summary: `isPrivateHost` loopback check is bypassed by a trailing-dot FQDN (`localhost.`), and by any private-network DNS name
finding.evidence: `LOOPBACK_HOSTS` is an exact-match set (`localhost`, ``, `[::1]`, `::1`) plus a `.localhost` suffix test (image-fetcher.ts:38,47). The WHATWG URL parser does not strip a trailing dot from a *domain* host (it only does so in the IPv4 parser when the host ends in a number), so `new URL('http://localhost./x').hostname === 'localhost.'` — which matches neither the set nor `.localhost`, is not an IPv4/IPv6 literal, and therefore falls through to `return false` (line 65) and is fetched. The OS resolver treats `localhost.` as the same name. Same shape for an attacker-chosen internal name (`metadata.google.internal`, an intranet host) — the comment at line 107 acknowledges DNS-resolved names, but a bare `localhost.` bypass of an explicitly enumerated loopback check is a hole in the check itself, not in DNS.

verdict.reason: The claimed bypass is not present. `isPrivateHost` normalizes the hostname with `.replace(/\.+$/, '')` before any comparison (packages/cli/src/docs/image-fetcher.ts:79-82), so `localhost.` becomes `localhost` and matches `LOOPBACK_HOSTS` (line 83), causing `assertFetchableImageUrl` to throw at lines 186-190. The comment at lines 75-78 names this exact trailing-root-label attack, and the allowlist path applies the same strip (lines 136-137). Tests at packages/cli/test/image-fetcher.test.ts:116-123 assert `localhost.`, `localhost..`, and `app.localhost.` all throw. The reviewer's cited evidence lines (38, 47, 65) do not contain the described code; `LOOPBACK_HOSTS` is line 67 and the fallthrough `return false` is line 101, after normalization. The second half of the claim (public DNS name resolving to a private address) is a real but explicitly documented scope limit at lines 160-162 requiring DNS resolution plus connection pinning below `fetch`; the reviewer concedes it is not a hole in the check, and the guard is re-applied on every redirect hop (line 241), so it is a hardening item rather than a blocking gate bypass.

searchedFor: grep for ${BASE}/${id} style interpolation in frontend/src/api
grep useParams call sites feeding workspaceId/token
finding.summary: Frontend `seg()` rule is applied only to `documents.ts`; every other API module still interpolates route-param ids raw into session-carrying URLs
finding.evidence: The change adds `packages/frontend/src/api/url.ts` and applies `seg()` in `documents.ts` only. Unencoded interpolation of ids that reach the browser from the URL bar remains at, among others: `api/workspaces.ts:184,196,212` (`${BASE}/${workspaceId}/api-keys`, POST/DELETE), `:102` (`members/${userId}`), `:143` (`invites/${inviteId}`), `api/folders.ts:10,24,42,64,82`, `api/share-links.ts:60,78,89,102`, `api/datasources.ts:45,65,78,90,104`, `api/analytics.ts:127`, `api/files.ts:22`, `app/spreadsheet/image-upload.ts:36`. Those ids are route params: `app/workspaces/workspace-settings.tsx:51` and `workspace-datasources.tsx:13` read `workspaceId` from `useParams`, `app/shared/shared-document.tsx:899` reads `token`. react-router percent-decodes params, so a crafted link such as `/workspaces/..%2F..%2Fauth%2Flogout/settings` makes `fetchWithAuth` issue the request against an endpoint the caller never named, with the victim's session attached (`fetch` resolves `..` per WHATWG). An added-but-partial gate reads as covered: the design doc it ships with states the rule is 'not CLI-only' while only the document routes actually enforce it.

verdict.reason: The finding claims `seg()` is applied only in `documents.ts` and that the listed modules still interpolate route-param ids raw. Every cited location actually calls `seg()`. In `packages/frontend/src/api/workspaces.ts` (the file the finding is filed on) `seg()` is used at 17 sites, covering exactly the lines called out as raw: api-keys at :185, :197, :213; `members/${seg(String(userId))}` at :103; `invites/${seg(inviteId)}` at :144; and the invite token at :157. The other cited modules are likewise covered: folders.ts:11,25,43,65,83; share-links.ts:61,79,90,103 (including the share token); datasources.ts:46,66,79,91,105; analytics.ts:128; files.ts:23 (with the `token` query param wrapped in encodeURIComponent at :24); image-upload.ts:48 (the cited :36 is `downscaleImageFile`, not a URL); miro.ts:94. A repo-wide grep for `VITE_BACKEND_API_URL`/`BACKEND_BASE`/`BASE}` shows the only remaining un-`seg`'d request URLs are fixed literal paths with no id interpolation (auth/*, notifications.ts:35/49/57/72, documents/move, documents/delete, analytics/enabled, /files). `seg()` at url.ts:18-23 rejects `.`/`..` and percent-encodes, so the described `/workspaces/..%2F..%2Fauth%2Flogout/settings` traversal is blocked at every named entry point. The code is not present as described.
